summary: Not a duplicate: norm-boundaries-persistent-multirow replaced the two 8192-wide FusedPostNormResidualPreNorm boundaries, and its 1.0716 came from master's own modules, because every Triton variant timed 12-39% slower in prepare. The decode and moe ports are per-token kernels for T<32, and moe's all-M variant lost or tied SGLang at bs=128/256. The expected ~0.3-0.5% per shape is well under the ±1.5% per-shape noise and the ±1.6% headline CI, so it can only be judged on the four replaced profile rows, and the spec must add a prepare-time timing gate and fix a likely weight double-add.
justification: Profile rows confirmed on master (archive/stack-tonight-five-prefill/c4d14d62f11e4aaf.profile.txt): _post_expert_norm_weighted_sum_kernel 8.2-8.9 / 23.8 / 119-130 us and at::native vectorized_layer_norm (pre_expert_norm) 6.6-6.8 / 18.0 / 77-79 us at T=753 / 3012 / 16384. Byte floors at first_turn: post-combine reads ~1/8 of 16384x8 slots (local routes) x 8 KB plus writes 134 MB, about 268 MB, so 56 us at 4.8 TB/s. The incumbent runs at ~2.2 TB/s, so this kernel has real headroom (practical ~4.0 TB/s means ~67 us, saving ~55 us). The pre-norm also moves 268 MB but already runs at ~3.4-3.5 TB/s, so the realistic saving is ~8-12 us. At turn_1 the inputs are L2-resident (pooler output is 6 MB) and both rows are latency-bound, so the HBM floors quoted (2.6 us) do not apply. Savings there are a few us at most. Total: ~65 us of 14.3-21.7 ms at first_turn (0.3-0.45%), ~15 us of 3.3-4.9 ms at turn_4, ~5-6 us of 1.1-1.5 ms at turn_1. Each is below the ±1.5% per-shape noise, so the headline cannot show it. That is acceptable only because both rows sit in the per-run profile.txt top list, which is archived for every run, so the rows are readable. WEAKEST LINK: the evidence that a hand-written Triton row kernel beats the incumbents at prefill M is negative. (a) In norm-boundaries-persistent-multirow's own prepare sweep (archive/norm-boundaries-persistent-multirow/46afe489e2754c83.log), rows-nw4, rows-nw8 and persistent-nw8 were 1.12-1.39x SLOWER than SGLang's CUDA kernel at every T, so the run executed master's modules. (b) The kernel to be copied, moe's _post_norm_combine_kernel, ran 4.5 us vs SGLang's 4.2 at bs=128 and 6.2 vs 6.4 at bs=256 (post-norm-triton-all-m). So it does not beat SGLang's Triton kernel as M grows, and the 1.130x cited is a T<32 result that does not transfer. The persistent multi-token restructuring is the untested part that has to deliver the gain. One structural point helps it: SGLang's kernel reaches only ~2.2 TB/s, likely from per-slot serialization, and the copied kernel's per-token loop over 8 slots with a scalar branch serializes 8 dependent row loads. For bandwidth, the new kernel should issue all local slots' loads before the reductions (moe's post-norm-combine-hoisted-slot-loads idea), not loop slot by slot.
confounders: stack-tonight-five-prefill (landed, current master a81d19c): its w2-nonlocal-zero-store-off part turns the w2 zero store off at T>4096 because _weighted_sum_skips_remote() proved SGLang's combine never reads remote y rows. The new combine replaces that kernel, so it inherits the precondition. The spec's NaN-in-remote-rows check covers it, but _weighted_sum_skips_remote still probes only SGLang's kernel. If the new kernel is ON, the probe (or a copy of it) must run against the new kernel, or a remote-row read becomes a silent correctness bug at first_turn only. The spec also says 'master (635cfee)'. Build on a81d19c and compare rows against c4d14d62f11e4aaf / 502f2eab95164781.

experts-hybrid-marlin-turn-triton-first-turn (landed): the combine has two call sites with different y producers. Marlin's moe_wna16_marlin_gemm output view at T<=4096, and the Triton engine's cache3 (a view into the shared cache13 buffer) at T>4096. topk_weights is cast to fp32 only on the Triton path. The kernel must accept both and take strides or contiguity explicitly. Otherwise a turn-shape result and a first_turn result may reflect different bugs or copies rather than the kernel.

router-hilo-one-gemm-n512 / moe-align parts of the stack: no interaction. They change routing-side launches that finish before _experts, and the combine's input set (local slots) is identical by construction.

sglang-pipeline-parity: defines post_expert_w as the module's effective (1 + w) weight in bf16. See rules_flags: moe's kernel adds 1.0 in-kernel to the ORIGINAL weight, so copying it verbatim while passing post_expert_w gives (2 + w). That is a numerical confounder that row-normalization partly masks.
interference: No companion. Both replaced kernels have their own rows in the archived profile.txt of every run (top list), so a gain or loss is read directly from four rows per shape against the c4d14d62f11e4aaf rows above, and nothing landed shares their launch or memory path except the remote-row precondition, which is a correctness question for prepare(), not an A/B question. Reverting any landed patch would either remove the y producer or change the remote-row contract, making the comparison worse, not cleaner. The pre-norm vs post-combine split does not need a separate run: they are separate rows. The run as specified does have one interpretability gap: it has no timing fallback. Given norm-boundaries' 12-39% Triton loss and moe's tie at bs=256, the run must carry its own prepare-time evidence. For each kernel separately and each T class (753, 3012, 16384), CUDA-graph-time the incumbent vs the new kernel with an L2 flush, median of >=25, and print '[moe-ends] pre|post T=... master X us new Y us'. Enable each kernel per T class only if <= 0.98x. Otherwise keep master's call for that kernel and class, and log which path was chosen. Then even an 'all OFF' run tells us something, as norm-boundaries' log did.
rules_flags: No rules problem in the mechanism. Effective weights are weight-derived constants computed in prepare(), as master already does. All math is fp32 with bf16 output, matching SGLang's precision. The work is in the timed call, there are no host syncs in kernel_fn, and nothing is cached from inputs.

Correctness hazard (not a rule break, but it could ship wrong numerics): the spec says copy moe's _post_norm_combine_kernel 'exact order of operations', which computes nw = w + 1.0 in-kernel from the ORIGINAL bf16 weight. But it also says to pass state['post_expert_w'], which is already the effective (1 + w). Pick one: pass weights['post_expert_norm'] and add 1 in fp32 (moe/decode convention), or pass post_expert_w and do not add 1. If w is near-constant, (2 + w) vs (1 + w) is mostly cancelled by the RMS normalization, so the rel L2 <= 1e-3 synthetic gate may not catch it. Make the gate use the REAL post_expert_norm weights and also a random w with std >= 0.1.

Gate metric: norm-boundaries' log shows its bf16 'max ulp' metric reporting 10^5-10^8 ulp at rel L2 ~2e-3, so an integer-reinterpretation ulp count is unreliable near zero and across signs. The spec's 'pre-norm max diff <= 1 bf16 ulp' risks a spurious OFF, which would mean measuring master again. Use max |diff| <= 1 ulp of |ref| per element (computed as float spacing, not bit distance) OR rel L2 <= 2e-3, and print the numbers.

After the change, the remote-slot contract must be re-probed against the kernel actually used (see confounders). Otherwise zero_nonlocal_w2=False plus a kernel that reads remote rows would produce NaN-dependent output on first_turn, which the 5 tests may not cover.
open_questions: Does a persistent multi-token combine that issues all local slots' row loads before the 8 reductions get the 16384 row below ~80 us? SGLang's Triton kernel sits at ~2.2 TB/s, and moe's per-token loop tied it at bs=256.

Is pre-expert norm worth replacing at all? At first_turn the incumbent is ~70% of the HBM floor, and at turn_1 it is L2- and latency-bound. If its prepare timing is not <= 0.98x, keep F.rms_norm and let the post-combine stand alone.

Longer term, the pre-norm belongs in the pooler GEMM's epilogue or the expert GEMM's A-load, and the combine in the w2 epilogue. Those fusions remove the 268 MB round trips that a standalone kernel can only shave.
